rationale: B wins because it has better evidence discipline. It keeps a real company-shape angle in "Going bets the cheap-fare alert is only the top of the trip" and admits "Honestly soft" on the $550 peg, while A lets "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" through with too little supplied fact underneath it. A has three usable angles, but B is less willing to decorate a hole and call it a narrative arc.
gaps_in_A: "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" overreaches. The update gives an old name and a launch, not a founder profile, timeline, or proven reinvention arc.

"consumer tech reporter at a general tech publication covering AI product launches" is too close to generic AI-launch mush. The stronger fit is travel-tech/product workflow, not the broad AI inbox where launches go to die.
"the prevailing model in AI travel tools is intent-first" may be true, but it is not in the supplied update. It needs outside market proof before it can carry the contrarian frame.

"using an AI itinerary planner to convert 2 million free members into paying subscribers" states the business intent too firmly. The facts support Premium-only gating, not proven conversion strategy or results.
gaps_in_B: "Mistake fares vanish fast" is plausible travel context, but it is not in the supplied facts. For this exercise, that is a borrowed peg until proved.
"If the prevailing push in the space is toward agents that book end-to-end" is an outside trend claim. B smartly flags the missing proof, but the angle still cannot be pitched without that evidence.

"$550 per flight: the savings number Going's paid tier rests on" is useful but soft. The number predates the planner in the supplied facts, so this is a methodology side story unless Going can tie it cleanly to the Premium pitch.
